articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite' (Digest No.53)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
abstract: One of the aims of EURACS, which is described, is to organise microwave and ancillary data in such a way as to reduce the potential data set in the eyes of the user. The EURACS database has been developed in response to a perceived need in Europe to rationalise research into microwave remote sensing. The database is designed to store radar cross section data and associated ground cover and instrument information. The development and installation of EURACS has been commissioned by the Institute of Applications at the Joint Research Centre (JRC), Ispra and has been undertaken by Hunting Technical Services Ltd in association with GEC-Marconi Research Centre. EURACS has been developed as a facility for use by researchers in microwave remote sensing, to assist research into backscatter modelling, algorithm development and sensor design. The EURACS database is a store of calibrated and validated radar cross section values and associated data, covering a full range of microwave sensors and platforms. The database also contains administrative information about the researchers involved in gathering the original data. This will enable any EURACS user to attempt to obtain further data at source, using compatible and comparable methods.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
abstract: Describes the design of a small satellite, named Innovative Modular Satellite (IMS), which resulted from a study conducted by MSS Ltd for the European Space Agency (ESA). The unique feature of the IMS system architecture is the collection of all service control functions within a single subsystem, the control subsystem, rather than the conventional architecture where control is spread throughout all the subsystems. This has advantages in that duplication of hardware is avoided and the overall control complexity is minimised with a consequent improvement in reliability and a reduction in software cost. This approach is facilitated on the IMS by the centralisation of most of the onboard service electronics in a single Service Electronics Rack (SER) and the intention to adopt a single source procurement philosophy at electrical system level.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: ERS data dissemination using VSAT systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
abstract: Dissemination of data and images produced by Earth Resource Sensing satellites must be distributed quickly to users in order to provide up-to-date information. The urgency and quantity of data associated with such information products are incompatible with existing mail services and facsimile or data networks. The paper describes the system requirements and architecture of a data distribution system, using very small aperture terminals (VSAT), which provides a solution to the problems associated with reception of bulk data products from the Earth Observation programmes.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
abstract: After a brief review of the SPOT system, as an example of utilization of an optical sensor, the paper briefly analyses the future optical sensors in low Earth orbits. The emphasis is put on the implications on data transmission and dissemination. The increasing demand for improved spatial and spectral resolutions have generated new concepts of sensors, such as imaging spectrometers. Two classes of instruments are envisaged as regard to the data transmission problem: instruments for global and continuous Earth monitoring and instruments for local high resolution applications. After a review of the current direct to ground link capability and its evolution, and a review of the recorders technology capability and limitation, some of the benefits from a data relay satellites system are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
abstract: The platform will provide a facility in low Earth, polar, Sun synchronous orbit offering standard resources such as power, data management, communications, pointing, to a wide variety of instruments and payload complements. It is modular in concept, comprising separately developed and integrated service and payload modules. Communications links are provided at S-band, at X-band for direct to ground transmission of payload data and at Ka-band via the European Data Relay Satellite (DRS) for commanding and for the transmission of instrument data. A brief description of the polar platform design is provided, focusing on some of the more critical areas which relate to challenging engineering or technology issues. An outline of the operational capabilities offered by the platform is also given showing the flexibility in operations afforded by the spacecraft design and the relationship with the DRS and ground segment infrastructures.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
abstract: Spaceborne active microwave sensors are briefly reviewed with reference to the 1978 Seasat satellite (for monitoring the oceans), and the European Remote Sensing Satellite, ERS-1, to be launched in 1990. The synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and wind scatterometer instruments are examined in more detail. User requirements for future SAR systems are considered. The impact of these requirements on the system is described. Some preliminary conclusions on the design of a future SAR are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Earth Resource Sensing and the Data Relay Satellite
abstract: The European Space Agency (ESA) is leading Europe in two major adventures in space, manned space flight and the exploration of the Earth. The manned space flight programme comprises Hermes, the European space plane, and Columbus, comprising both free-flying attached European elements of the International Space Station Freedom. The Earth exploration programme of the Agency will comprise a series of Polar Platforms In addition, European national space agencies plan to fly their own Earth exploration satellites. To support this In-Orbit Infrastructure, ESA has started development of a new space telecommunications network, based on the European Data Relay System, DRS.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
